newsitem.title: USA: Cancer gene may not be DNA "policeman".
newsitem.headline: Cancer gene may not be DNA "policeman".

text.p: Researchers on Wednesday raised fundamental questions about precisely what role a crucial gene nicknamed "Guardian of the genome" plays in causing cancer.

The research, led by molecular biologist Garth Anderson at Roswell Park Cancer Institute in Buffalo, New York, does not rule out a key role for the p53 gene -- one of the hottest areas of cancer research -- but defies the conventional wisdom about what that role is, and when it kicks in.

The research, to appear in the Nov. 20 issue of the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, involves colorectal cancer but Anderson said that scientists in his lab are seeing similar results in other malignancies.
"We sort of feel like the lightbulb is going on," he said in a telephone interview. "People were looking at p53 as the start of a 1,000 step journey. It's more like step 999."

P53 is often called the "guardian" or the "policeman" of the genome, the collection of genetic information. Under that scenario, when something goes wrong with p53 the result is cellular havoc, a domino-effect of mutations that eventually gives rise to cancer.
But Anderson's research questions that sequence, although it does not dispute that p53 is involved in many cancers. "People were giving more credit to this molecule than it deserves," he said.

Anderson does not think it is the "policeman," guarding against what scientists call genomic instability, or what a layperson might think of as scrambled genetic information. "It's not the thing that allows the dominos to start falling down," he said.
Anderson likens genomic instability to an audiotape that has lots of information on it but is then randomly cut and spliced back together.
"If you listened to it, you'd still get noise ... but you would't get music," he said.

Anderson is now working on research that will present an alternative mechanism for genome instability. Understanding how the process that leads to cancer occurs could eventually lead to ways of preventing it.
